This guide walks you through building one FlexiTac-V2 sensor (32 × 12 taxels), connecting it to a 32 × 16 reading board , and streaming it live to a heatmap on your computer. This is the standard setup: the fabrication guide, the firmware and PyFlexiTac all default to it. Each step links to a detailed page. Generate the two FPCs for your own gripper or fingertip with FlexiTac-Gen . It also tells you which reading board fits your design. Ordering and fabrication work the same way. You need three things for a FlexiTac-V2 setup: the two sensor FPCs and the reading board from a PCB manufacturer, plus a few off-the-shelf parts (Arduino Nano, cables, consumables). Fabrication takes 1–2 weeks including shipping, so order everything at once. This page summarizes the FlexiTac Hardware Fabrication Guide ↗ (March 2026). If anything here disagrees with the guide, follow the guide, and please report it ↗ so we can fix this page.

Fabricating a FlexiTac-V2 sensor is mostly lamination: no soldering, and no special tools beyond scissors or a craft knife. Once you have done it once, a sensor takes under three minutes. The steps below follow the fabrication video ↗ . It's worth watching once before your first build.

Everything for one sensor: the top and bottom FPCs, adhesive lamination sheets, Velostat and polyimide tape. Item BOM # Notes Top FPC and bottom FPC 1 One of each per sensor Adhesive laminating sheets 4 Two pre-cut pieces, one per FPC Velostat / Linqstat 3 One piece that covers the electrode area Polyimide tape 2 For sealing the edges FFC extenders (16- and 32-pin) and flat cables 7–12 For connecting to the reading board in step 4 Assembled reading board 5–6 Flashed or not; you can flash it later See Order parts for the full bill of materials.

A FlexiTac sensor is five thin layers. Both FPCs turn their copper electrodes toward the Velostat in the middle: the top FPC's 12 columns face down and the bottom FPC's 32 rows face up. Wherever a row crosses a column there is a taxel, and pressing it squeezes the film between the two electrodes. 1 2 3 4 5 Laminating sheet holds the top FPC from behind. Top FPC : 12 column electrodes, copper side down. You see its back here, with the copper showing through. Velostat : the pressure-sensitive film, cut to cover the electrode area. Bottom FPC : 32 row electrodes, copper side up. Laminating sheet

Attach each FPC to a lamination sheet and align it Peel a pre-cut lamination sheet and attach the top FPC to it. Do the same with the bottom FPC on a second sheet. Align the corners exactly, as in the photos: the two layers must line up when you stack them in step 2. Peel the lamination sheet. Place the FPC, corners aligned. One laminated FPC layer. Stack the Velostat between the two layers Place the Velostat in the middle, between the two prepared layers, centered over the electrode area. Close the stack with the second layer. Once it's centered, the sensor stack already works. Center the Vel

Fully seat the gold fingers. Push each FPC end all the way into its connector, straight and not skewed. A finger that's half-seated or off by one pin is the most common cause of dead or swapped rows. Mind the cable orientation. FFC contacts are on one side only. If a whole sensor reads nothing, check that each cable's contacts face the connector contacts at both ends. The Adafruit extenders need practice. They're compact but take careful alignment. The AliExpress extenders (BOM #12) are bulkier but easier to install. Keep the Velostat covering every crossing. Your sensor is wired to the reading board. Now stream the sensor .

The Arduino Nano on the reading board runs a small sketch that scans the sensor and streams frames over USB. Flash it once, then watch a bright spot follow your finger on a live heatmap. That's a working sensor.

Get the sketch Download PyFlexiTac's firmware sketch ↗ ( Download raw file on that page) and open it in the Arduino IDE ↗ . Let the IDE move it into a folder of the same name. It is already set up for the V2 sensor: 12 rows, 32 columns, 2,000,000 baud. Select the board and port Tools → Board → Arduino AVR Boards → Arduino Nano , then pick the serial port under Tools → Port . If the upload fails with not in sync , set Tools → Processor → ATmega328P (Old Bootloader) and try again. Upload Click Upload . You only need to do this once per board.

Start with flexitac-stream --port <port> . Its output (fps, raw_max , norm_max ) tells you which layer is failing: USB and serial, firmware, or the sensor itself.

Try another USB cable. Many mini-USB cables only carry power. If the Nano's LED lights up but no port appears, the cable is the most likely cause. Check the USB driver. Many Nano clones use a CH340 USB-serial chip. Recent Linux and macOS versions include a driver. On older systems, install the CH340 driver from the chip vendor. Look at the kernel log (Linux) while you plug the board in: On Linux, brltty can grab CH340 devices. If the port appears and immediately disappears, removing that package ( sudo apt remove brltty ) is a common fix.
Your user can't open the serial device. On Linux, add yourself to dialout and log in again: See Serial port permissions for macOS and temporary workarounds.

The port opens, but the reader never finds a start marker ( 0xAA 0x55 ) followed by a full frame. Re-flash. A board fresh from the factory, or one running another sketch, isn't sending FlexiTac frames. Check the baud rate. Both sides must use 2,000,000 unless you changed it on purpose. At the wrong rate, the bytes arrive garbled and no marker is ever found. Check the port. Make sure you're reading the reading board and not another serial device. flexitac-find-port tells you which one it is. Close other programs that might be reading the same port (serial monitor, a second script).

h: The heatmap looks scrambled or shifted
x: Frames arrive, but the picture is wrong. This usually means a row-count mismatch between the firmware you flashed and the reader: What you see Cause Fix Normal fps, but the top 4 rows never respond and touches near one end of the sensor don't show Firmware sends 16 rows ( 32_16_fast.ino ), reader expects 12 Read with --rows 16 , or flash PyFlexiTac's sketch instead Frame rate drops to about half, and the bottom 4 rows echo touches on the top rows Firmware sends 12 rows, reader expects 16 Read with the defaults (12 rows) A round touch shows up as a slanted streak (each row shifted a little furt

h: Some rows or columns never respond
x: Run flexitac-stream --port <port> --per-row and press along a column. Then check: Gold fingers fully and squarely seated in each FFC connector. Re-seat both ends and both cables. Cable orientation. A cable inserted with its contacts facing the wrong way gives a whole dead side. Velostat coverage. A dead band along one edge often means the film doesn't reach that edge. Lamination alignment. If the top and bottom FPCs were offset when you stacked them, edge crossings may not overlap. Expected dead rows: with 32_16_fast.ino on a V2 sensor, rows 0–3 are unconnected by design. Swap parts to isolate

A value that stays flat at either end of the range points to a wiring problem , such as a disconnected or shorted line, not a flashing problem. Re-seat the connectors and inspect the gold fingers and cables for damage.

Re-calibrate with nothing touching the sensor. If the sensor was pressed during the first ~30 frames, the baseline is wrong. Call sensor.calibrate() or restart the stream. Mounting changes the baseline. Bending or pre-loading the sensor onto a curved finger raises its resting values. Calibrate after mounting, not before. Expect small fluctuations. normalized hides readings below the threshold (default 25 counts above baseline). If you work with raw , apply your own threshold or temporal filter. The hardware repo's fast_32_16.py uses an exponential filter with α = 0.2.

h: The signal saturates or barely changes
x: Saturates under light touch: the sensor may be pre-loaded by its mount, or the baseline was captured under load. Re-calibrate at rest. Barely changes under firm pressure: check that the Velostat is present and centered, and that the polyimide seal isn't holding the layers apart. Make sure you're reading the right port, and not another device.

About 100+ fps is expected for 12 × 32 at 2 Mbaud. Lower rates usually come from a slow USB hub, a very busy host, or a visualizer that renders every frame. For live use, call read_latest() so rendering never falls behind.

h: How long do FPC and PCB orders take?
x: Usually 1–2 weeks from order to delivery for the FPCs and PCBs, depending on your location and shipping method. An assembled reading board takes about one week.
In the authors' experience, sensors stay consistent and can often be used for about a year without significant degradation. Some teams have collected thousands of demonstrations without breaking one.

h: What if a sensor is damaged or malfunctioning?
x: Order a few spare sensors up front. Replacing a damaged sensor with a new one typically doesn't noticeably affect performance, so sensors are consistent across instances.

A tactile demonstration records what the sensor feels, what the camera sees and what the gripper does, all at the same moments. There are two ways to collect one. Teleoperation Drive a robot arm and record from the robot itself. One sensor, on the moving jaw. UMI data Hold the gripper and do the task yourself, anywhere, no robot needed. A sensor on each finger. New to robot learning? Start with teleoperation. It is the lowest-cost setup and uses the sensor exactly as these docs set it up.

You move a leader arm and the follower robot copies it, so the recorded actions are the robot's own. The open setup is LeFlexiTac ↗ , which adds FlexiTac to LeRobot ↗ on the low-cost SO-100/101 arm. You hold a UMI ↗ -style gripper and do the task yourself, indoors or outdoors, with no robot. A GoPro on the gripper records vision, and a FlexiTac sensor on each soft finger records touch. The open setup is Touch in the Wild ↗ (NeurIPS 2025). Its authors used it to collect more than 2,700 demonstrations across 43 tasks in 12 environments. Mount on something slightly soft, such as a fin-ray finger, so contact spreads over several taxels. Keep the cable still at the connector. Route the flat cable so it doesn't flex while the gripper moves. Calibrate after mounting. The mount itself changes the resting baseline. Keep touch in sync. LeFlexiTac records touch into the same dataset frames as the camera and joints, so train and run a policy at the frame rate you recorded at. 3D-ViTac ↗ (CoRL 2024) is where this line of work started. It introduced the sensor now called FlexiTac-V1 and the visuo-tactile point cloud , which places each taxel in 3D next to the camera points and feeds both to one policy. For now its training-code repository ↗ only points to the pre-training stage of VT-Refine . The authors say that stage uses the same setup but runs in simulation, on VT-Refine's plug–socket data rather than 3D-ViTac's own tasks. 3D-ViTac's data and real-robot code have not been released yet. For more work built on FlexiTac, see Awesome FlexiTac ↗ .

LeFlexiTac trains policies on the LeRobot datasets you record with it . Touch is an extra input, switched on with --policy.use_tactile=true . On tube insertion, peg-in-hole and pen retrieval from a bag, the tactile policies beat their vision-only versions in every reported comparison ( results ↗ ). Train with and without touch ( --policy.use_tactile=true / false ) on a Linux machine with a CUDA GPU, then roll the checkpoint out on the arm. x: Touch in the Wild trains a Diffusion Policy conditioned on its pretrained visuo-tactile encoder , then runs it on a uFactory xArm 850 with the same fingers and sensors. The simulation lets you work with touch without any hardware. Simulated pads give the same 12 × 32 taxel grid as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor, on the fingers of a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The current release is the FlexiTac tactile simulation in Isaac Sim , which this page shows you how to build and run. It uses the same bimanual plug–socket setup and the same pad layout as VT-Refine , the research on fine-tuning visuo-tactile policies in simulation, whose own code runs on the older Isaac Gym. x: Start the web interface, then open http://localhost:8080 : Drag the handle on each end effector to move the two arms, and open or close each gripper with its buttons. Each file holds: Key Shape What it is tactile (T, 4, 12, 32) The four pads, in the order left arm left finger, left arm

Each finger has a pad with a 12 × 32 grid of taxels at 2 mm pitch, the same layout as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor. On every step, NVIDIA Warp ↗ measures how far each taxel has pushed into the object's mesh. That depth becomes a spring force, clamp(stiffness × depth, 0, max_force) , which is then divided by max_force so each reading lies between 0 and 1. The grid size, spacing, stiffness (5000) and max_force (10) are settings in AlohaTactileEnvCfg ↗ . The pads on the left arm sense only the socket, and the pads on the right arm only the plug. Touching anything else, such as the table, gives no signal.

VT-Refine ↗ (CoRL 2025) trains bimanual assembly policies in three stages, from real to sim and back to real. It first trains a diffusion policy on about 30 real demonstrations per task. Each demonstration records FlexiTac pads on all four fingers together with a camera point cloud, the representation from 3D-ViTac . Next it fine-tunes that policy in a simulated copy of the setup with large-scale, GPU-parallel reinforcement learning. Finally it moves the policy back to the real robot. PyFlexiTac ↗ is the flexitac Python package (MIT-licensed, maintained by Wesley Maa). Stream the sensor already used it for the live heatmap. This page covers the rest. Its README is the source of truth for every option.
PyFlexiTac needs Python 3.11 or newer . pip uv From source This installs four commands: flexitac-find-port , flexitac-heatmap , flexitac-stream and flexitac-flash .

flexitac-stream prints the frame rate and signal statistics. It tells you whether the board, the firmware and the reader agree. On its first read, PyFlexiTac calibrates : it collects 30 frames and stores each taxel's median as the baseline. If you press the sensor during calibration, that pressure becomes part of the "zero." Each frame is a FlexiTacFrame : Field Type Meaning seq int Frame counter since the sensor was opened timestamp_s float Host time when the frame was read ( time.time() ) raw uint8[rows, cols] Values exactly as sent by the firmware normalized float32[rows, cols] Baseline-subtracted, thresholded and scaled to 0–1 Useful methods and options: sensor.read() returns the next frame in order. Use it when you're recording data and don't want to skip any. sensor.read_latest() discards queued frames and returns the newest one. Use it for live control or visualization , so you never lag behind the sensor.

Each reading board is its own USB serial device. For a two-finger gripper, open one FlexiTacSensor per port (find each with flexitac-find-port ) and read them in parallel threads, or call read_latest() on each in your control loop.

flexitac-flash puts the same sketch on the board as the Arduino IDE path, without opening the IDE, and can generate it for a custom sensor size. If you're writing your own reader, for a robot middleware, a microcontroller or another language, here is the whole protocol. For every frame, the firmware sends a two-byte start marker, then selects each row through a 16-channel analog multiplexer, steps through each column with shift registers, and reads each crossing with the Nano's 10-bit ADC, scaled to one byte. Field Value Transport USB serial, 2,000,000 baud , 8N1 Start marker 2 bytes: 0xAA 0x55 Payload rows × cols bytes, unsigned 8-bit, row-major (row 0 first, columns 0…cols−1) Value ADC reading ÷ 4 (10-bit → 8-bit).
